passages.t: He is not here; He has risen
passages.happening:
After the Sabbath, at dawn on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary go to see the tomb. Suddenly there is a great earthquake. An angel of the Lord comes down from heaven, rolls away the stone, and sits on it. He looks like lightning, and his clothes are white as snow. The guards shake with fear and become like dead men.

The angel says to the women, “Do not be afraid, for I know that you are looking for Jesus, who was crucified. He is not here; He has risen, just as He said! Come, see the place where He lay” (verses 5-6). He tells them to go quickly and tell the disciples that Jesus has risen and is going ahead of them into Galilee.

The women hurry away from the tomb, afraid and full of joy, and run to tell the disciples. Suddenly Jesus meets them. “Greetings!” he says. They come to him, take hold of his feet, and worship him. “Do not be afraid,” Jesus says. “Go and tell My brothers to go to Galilee. There they will see Me” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Mark tells of the empty tomb too (Mark 16:1-8), and the note on Mark 16 explains the burial customs and the first day of the week, which became the day Christians gather.

In that world, a woman's word counted for less than a man's. Josephus, writing near the end of the first century, says that under Jewish law the testimony of women was not to be accepted (Antiquities 4.219). In the second century a critic of Christianity named Celsus mocked the resurrection as resting on the word of ‘a half-frantic woman’, as Origen reports in his reply. Yet all four Gospels agree that women were the first to find the tomb empty. Many historians think a story made up to convince people would hardly have chosen these witnesses. Matthew had already said that these same women watched Jesus die and sat facing his tomb (27:56, 27:61).

Matthew tells the morning in his own way. Only Matthew has the earthquake, the angel rolling the stone and sitting on it, and the guards falling down like dead men. The men posted to keep a dead man in the tomb become like dead men themselves. The angel does not roll the stone away to let Jesus out. He rolls it away to let the women see in.

And only Matthew tells that Jesus himself met the women on the road. They take hold of his feet. He is not a ghost or a vision. And he calls the disciples who ran away ‘My brothers’.
passages.ot:
Jesus had told the disciples more than once that he would be killed and “on the third day be raised to life” (16:21; also 17:23 and 20:19). On the night he was betrayed he said, “after I have risen, I will go ahead of you into Galilee” (26:32). The angel says, “just as He said.”

The prophets had hoped for a day when God “will swallow up death forever” (Isaiah 25:8), and Daniel saw that “many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake” (Daniel 12:2). Many Jews expected God to raise the dead at the end of time. No one expected one man to be raised in the middle of history, ahead of everyone else.

The angel's face like lightning recalls the heavenly figure Daniel saw, whose face was “like the brilliance of lightning” (Daniel 10:6).
passages.hard:
Why do the four Gospels tell Easter morning differently? They do, and it is better to say so plainly. Matthew names Mary Magdalene and ‘the other Mary’; Mark adds Salome; Luke names Joanna and others; John tells of Mary Magdalene alone. Matthew and Mark speak of one angel, Luke and John of two. Matthew and Mark point to meetings in Galilee; Luke tells only of appearances in and near Jerusalem; John has both.

Christians have explained this in more than one way. Many hold that each writer chose some of the events and left others out, so that the accounts can be fitted together, for example with the first appearances in Jerusalem and later ones in Galilee. Others think some details simply cannot be fitted together with confidence, and that this is what honest reports of a shocking morning look like. Witnesses who agree in every detail are often suspected of having agreed on a story. Skeptics see the differences as signs of legend growing.

What every account agrees on is the centre. Jesus died and was buried. On the first day of the week women found the tomb empty. They were told he had risen. And he appeared to his followers. Paul, writing in the 50s, already lists witnesses who saw him (1 Corinthians 15:3-8).
passages.asks: The women went to the tomb to care for the dead. They left it running to tell the living. Matthew says they were afraid and full of joy at the same time. Ask whether you have ever felt both. And notice Jesus' first words to them: ‘Do not be afraid.’ Then he sends them to the men who had run away, and he calls those men ‘My brothers’. The first word of Easter in Matthew is a welcome home for people who failed.

passages.happening:
While the women are on their way, some of the guards go into the city and tell the chief priests everything that has happened. The chief priests meet with the elders and make a plan. They give the soldiers a large sum of money and tell them, “You are to say, ‘His disciples came by night and stole Him away while we were asleep’” (verse 13). If the governor hears of it, they will satisfy him and keep the soldiers out of trouble.

So the guards take the money and do as they are told. Matthew adds, “And this account has been circulated among the Jews to this very day” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
Only Matthew tells this, and it finishes the story of the guard he began in 27:62-66.

Notice what the soldiers are paid to say. They are to say they were asleep. Soldiers who said they slept on duty were admitting a serious failure, which is why the priests promise to protect them (verse 14). And the story undercuts itself. If they were asleep, how could they know who took the body?

‘To this very day’ means the day Matthew was writing, some decades later. The rumour that the disciples stole the body was still being told. A Christian writer of the second century, Justin Martyr, says in his Dialogue with Trypho that the same charge was still being spread in his time (Dialogue 108).

‘Among the Jews’ needs careful reading. Matthew himself was a Jew, and so were Jesus, the women, the disciples and the first churches. Here he means the people outside the church who told this story, as a rumour he is answering. He is describing an argument of his own day about what happened to the body. It is not a statement about Jewish people as a whole, and it must never be read as one. On the misuse of the passion story against the Jewish people, see the note on 27:15-26.
passages.ot: The Old Testament knows that the powerful can pay to have the truth hidden. The law warned, “Do not accept a bribe, for a bribe blinds those who see and twists the words of the righteous” (Exodus 23:8). Matthew's story began with silver paid for a betrayal (26:15) and ends with silver paid for a lie.
passages.hard:
What does the rumour show? Both sides of the argument agreed that the tomb was empty. The disciples said he had risen. Their opponents said the body was stolen. No one in the story says the body is still in the tomb. The argument was over why it was empty, not whether.

Could the disciples have stolen the body? Skeptics have raised this ever since. Others answer that the disciples had run away in fear, and that soon afterwards they were jailed and flogged for what they said they had seen (Acts 5:18, 5:40). People will suffer for what they believe is true. It is much harder to see why a group would suffer for a story they knew they had made up. The theft story does not explain the appearances that the first Christians reported. These notes set out the question; the reader is trusted to weigh it.
passages.asks: The priests paid money to bury the truth a second time. Ask whether there are truths you would rather pay to keep quiet: about yourself, your past, or about Jesus. The empty tomb could not be explained away by a story told for money. Ask what you will do with it.

passages.t: On the mountain: they worshipped, but some doubted
passages.happening: The eleven disciples go to Galilee, to the mountain Jesus had told them about, just as the angel and Jesus himself had said they should. Matthew tells what happens in one short sentence: “When they saw Him, they worshiped Him, but some doubted” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
There are only eleven now. Judas is gone. Matthew does not hide the gap.

Mountains matter in Matthew. Jesus was tempted on a very high mountain, where the devil offered him all the kingdoms of the world if he would worship him (4:8-9). He taught the Sermon on the Mount (5:1). He was transfigured on a high mountain (17:1-2). Now, on a mountain in Galilee, he will claim all authority, not as a gift from the devil but from his Father.

‘Some doubted’ is an honest line. The Greek word for ‘doubt’ here is used only one other time in the New Testament: when Peter walked on the water and began to sink, and Jesus said, “You of little faith,” “why did you doubt?” (14:31). There it meant hesitating, being of two minds, not a settled refusal to believe. Peter doubted while Jesus was holding him up.

Who doubted? The Greek can be read as ‘some of the eleven doubted’, or as speaking of others who were there too. Many readers take it to mean some of the eleven. Either way, Matthew puts doubt and worship side by side on the very mountain where the Gospel ends.
passages.ot: Mountains in the Old Testament are places where God meets his people and gives his word. At Mount Sinai God gave Moses the law, and before that he told Moses at the burning bush, “I will surely be with you,” and that the people would “worship God on this mountain” (Exodus 3:12). Matthew's last scene is on a mountain too, with worship, a commission, and a promise of presence.
passages.hard:
Why would anyone doubt while looking at the risen Jesus? Matthew does not say. Some think the doubt was hesitation: fear, wonder, and not knowing how to approach him after they had run away. Others think it was the slowness of the mind to take in something so new, as when Luke says the apostles thought the women's words “seemed like nonsense” (Luke 24:11).

What matters most is what Jesus does next. He does not wait for the doubters to sort themselves out. He comes to them (verse 18). He gives his command to the whole group, doubters included. Matthew does not make faith a condition for being sent.

This gives a doubting reader room. The first followers of Jesus did not believe easily. They saw him and some still hesitated. Doubt is not the opposite of worship here; it stands right beside it. A father in Mark's Gospel once prayed, “I do believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24). Jesus did not turn him away either. If you are carrying doubts, you are in the company of the eleven. Bring them with you.
passages.asks: Matthew could have ended with every disciple full of faith. He wrote ‘some doubted’. Ask whether you have thought that doubt disqualifies you from following Jesus. On this mountain the doubters were still there, still worshipping, and still sent. Ask what it would mean to worship with your questions rather than wait until they are gone.

passages.t: Make disciples of all nations; I am with you always
passages.happening:
Jesus comes to them and says, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me. Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey all that I have commanded you. And surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age” (verses 18-20).

That is where Matthew ends. There is no departure scene. The last word is a promise.
passages.hearers:
‘All authority’ is a royal claim. Daniel had seen one like a son of man given “dominion, glory, and kingship” (Daniel 7:14). The one who was mocked as king a few days before now claims authority over heaven and earth.

‘All nations’ is a turn in the story. When Jesus first sent out the Twelve, he told them, “Do not go onto the road of the Gentiles” and “Go rather to the lost sheep of Israel” (10:5-6). He said of himself, “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (15:24). Now the circle opens to everyone. Scholars discuss whether ‘all nations’ here means only the non-Jewish peoples or every people including Israel. Many read it as every people. Either way, the good news that began in Israel is now for the whole world. Matthew has been pointing this way since the wise men from the east came to worship (2:1-2) and since Jesus said that many would come from east and west to the feast (8:11).

To ‘make disciples’ is more than to win converts. A disciple is a learner who follows a teacher and lives the way he lives. That is why Jesus adds ‘teaching them to obey all that I have commanded you’. The five long teachings of Matthew are what the disciples are to pass on.

The threefold name was used very early. The Didache, a church manual from around AD 100, gives the same words for baptism: in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. It prefers running water and allows water to be poured three times on the head if there is not enough water for more (Didache 7).
passages.ot:
God promised Abraham, “through your offspring all nations of the earth will be blessed” (Genesis 22:18). Matthew's book began by calling Jesus “the son of Abraham” (1:1). It ends with that blessing sent to all nations.

The promise ‘I am with you’ is God's promise to those he sends. To Moses he said, “I will surely be with you” (Exodus 3:12). To Joshua: “the LORD your God is with you wherever you go” (Joshua 1:9). Jesus now speaks as God spoke.
passages.hard:
How should baptism be done, and who should receive it? Christians answer differently, and the differences are long-standing. Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican, Reformed, Methodist and other churches baptize the infants of believers as well as adults, seeing baptism as God's gift and promise given to families too. Baptists and many other churches baptize only those old enough to confess faith for themselves, seeing baptism as the believer's public response to the gospel. Churches also differ on whether to immerse, pour or sprinkle, and on how far baptism is a means by which God gives grace or a sign that follows it. Acts speaks of baptism ‘in the name of Jesus Christ’ (Acts 2:38), and most churches read that as describing Christian baptism rather than giving a different form of words. These notes do not settle these questions. All these churches agree that Jesus commanded his followers to baptize, and that baptism joins a person to Christ and to his people (Romans 6:4).

The words ‘the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit’ name one God: ‘in the name’, not ‘in the names’. The church's teaching on the Trinity, set out in the creeds, was put into words later, but Christians have always seen it rooted in verses like this one.
passages.asks: Matthew's Gospel began with a promise: “they will call Him Immanuel” (which means, “God with us”) (1:23). It ends with the same promise in Jesus' own mouth: “I am with you always, even to the end of the age.” Everything in between, the teaching, the miracles, the cross and the empty tomb, sits inside that promise. Jesus did not send the disciples out alone, and he did not send them out because they were ready. Some of them were still doubting. Ask where you are being sent: your home, your street, your work. And ask what it would change to believe, on an ordinary day, that he is with you.
